newsitem.title: USA: North Korean apology for incursion praised by U.S..
newsitem.headline: North Korean apology for incursion praised by U.S..

text.p: North Korea's belated apology for a submarine intrusion into South Korea drew praise from President Bill Clinton on Sunday and raised hopes that the two Koreas, the United States and China would hold peace talks.
Clinton welcomed Pyongyang's expression of "deep regret" as a significant development and said he hoped discussions could go ahead on the four-party talks proposed by Washington and Seoul last April.

The submarine incident, in which 26 heavily armed North Koreans landed after running aground on a South Korean beach on Sept. 18, interrupted a process of engagement intended to bring Pyongyang out of isolation, revamp its nuclear programme and help ease a famine in North Korea.

South Korea branded the incursion a military provocation and demanded an apology from the North. For more than three months, the United States had pressed Pyongyang to comply, warning that a series of diplomatic deals and the proposed peace talks were being jeopardised by the delay.

The brief statement of apology and a promise the incident would not be repeated were issued after U.S. and North Korean officials hammered out acceptable wording during intense negotiating sessions in New York that began almost three weeks ago.
Those talks wound up over the weekend, when envoys agreed on a choice of words for a public apology they felt would satisy South Korea, U.S. officials said.

The United States now is hopeful Seoul and Pyongyang can put the submarine incident behind them and move ahead on improving relations and reducing tensions on the Korean peninsula, the officials added.
Clinton thanked South Korean President Kim Young-sam for his personal efforts to resolve the issue "in a way that opens the door for future South-North dialogue."

"I am pleased that Pyongyang has pledged to prevent the recurrence of such an incident and has expressed its willingness to work with others for durable peace and stability on the Peninsula," he said in a written statement.
"I hope discussions can now begin to move forward on the four-party peace talks which President Kim Young-sam and I offered last April," Clinton said.
Officials and diplomats in New York and Washington expected the apology to set in motion a series of measures over the coming months.

These could include a pledge from South Korea to resume contruction work soon on two civilian nuclear reactors in the North and a simultaneous promise from North Korea to resume disposing of spent nuclear fuel rods.

Under a 1994 accord, North Korea agreed to give up its suspected atomic weapons programme in exchange for oil and a set of light-water reactors. But when Seoul put the project on hold after the submarine incursion, Pyongyang responded by halting work on overhauling its nuclear programme.
International food aid to economically devastated North Korea, which had been frozen by three months of rising tensions on the peninsula, also could begin flowing again, officials said.
The U.N. World Food Programme planned to issue another appeal in the next few weeks. The United States may then pledge about $6 million in famine assistance.

The four-party peace talks proposed by Clinton and Kim during the U.S. president's visit to South Korea earlier this year would seek to secure a lasting peace to replace the truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
